system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2179-05-16 04:18:00 to 2179-05-20 14:33:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with primary sclerosing cholangitis, cirrhosis, and a history of recurrent cholangitis was admitted for right upper quadrant abdominal pain, low-grade fever, and malaise. She had completed a course of meropenem for a prior cholangitis episode two weeks earlier. Initial concern was for recurrent cholangitis, so she was started on meropenem again. Imaging showed no bile duct dilation, abscess, or dominant stricture, and cultures were negative. The infectious disease team concluded this was not acute cholangitis but recommended completing a short course of antibiotics given her history. Her symptoms resolved, liver enzymes improved, and she remained afebrile. Diuretics were held initially but resumed at discharge. She was discharged home with plans to complete IV antibiotics via her PICC line, continue all home medications, and follow up for liver clinic visits and a colonoscopy. Her transplant status remains unchanged.
problems: Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  MRCP

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with known cirrhosis and history of cholangitis
// Any acute cholangitis? any pathology to explain fevers and RUQ pain?

TECHNIQUE:  T1- and T2-weighted multiplanar images of the abdomen were
acquired in a 1.5 T magnet.
Intravenous contrast: 7 mL Gadavist.
Oral contrast:  1 cc of Gadavist mixed with 50 cc of water was administered
for oral contrast.

The patient was pre-medicated as per departmental protocol for known allergy
to MR contrast.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal ultrasound ___.  CT abdomen and pelvis ___.  Most recent MRCP from ___.

FINDINGS: 

Lower Thorax: Lower lung bases and pleural spaces are clear.  Multiple
paraesophageal and gastric varices are again noted.

Liver: Liver demonstrates background morphological changes of cirrhosis with
areas of confluent fibrosis.  No focal liver lesions.  Hepatic vasculature
remains patent.  Gallstones are again seen within the remnant gallbladder. 
Small volume ascites.

Biliary: Again noted is prominence and irregularity of the intrahepatic
biliary tree, as seen previously, in keeping with the provided history of
primary sclerosing cholangitis.  On the post contrast images there is
progressive enhancement around the walls of the intrahepatic biliary tree, as
seen previously, again due to chronic cholangitis and fibrosis.  No
extrahepatic ductal dilatation.  Inter sphincteric portion of the common bile
duct again is not visualized, a finding which may suggest Sphincter of Oddi
dysfunction.

Pancreas: Pancreas demonstrates normal signal intensity with no focal mass,
ductal dilatation or peripancreatic abnormality.

Spleen: The spleen is enlarged, measuring up to 13 cm in the CC dimension.  No
focal mass.

Adrenal Glands: Adrenal glands are normal in appearance.

Kidneys: No dilatation of the collecting system.  No focal renal masses.  No
perinephric abnormalities.

Gastrointestinal Tract:  No dilated loops of bowel.  Again noted involving the
right the colon is mild wall thickening and mural edema, as seen previously,
likely relating to underlying portal hypertension.

Lymph Nodes: No mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.

Vasculature: No aneurysmal dilatation of the abdominal aorta.  Multiple upper
abdominal varices are again noted.

Osseous and Soft Tissue Structures: No acute or aggressive osseous lesions.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  Background hepatic cirrhosis with small volume ascites, splenomegaly, and
upper abdominal varices in keeping with sequelae of portal hypertension.  No
concerning focal mass.

2.  Prominence and irregularity of the intrahepatic biliary tree, as seen
previously, in keeping with provided history of primary sclerosing
cholangitis.  No MR features of acute cholangitis.

3.  Right colonic wall edema, as seen previously, likely relates to portal
colopathy.

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with PSC and suspected hepatobilliary infection
being treated with meropenem. Has history of 14 PICCs, previous attempts
unsuccessful  // PICC line placement

COMPARISON:  None.

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___, Interventional Radiology Fellow and Dr.
___, attending radiologist performed the procedure. Dr. ___
___ personally supervised the trainee during the key components of the
procedure and has reviewed and agrees with the trainee's findings.
ANESTHESIA: 1% lidocaine was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues
overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: None.
CONTRAST: None
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  0.3 min, 0 mGy

PROCEDURE:
1. Single lumen PICC placement through the basilic vein on the right.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, the basilic
vein on the right was punctured under direct ultrasound guidance using a
micropuncture set. Permanent ultrasound images were obtained before and after
intravenous access, which confirmed vein patency. A peel-away sheath was then
placed over a guidewire. The guidewire was then advanced into the superior
vena cava using fluoroscopic guidance. A single lumen PIC line measuring 43 cm
in length was then placed through the peel-away sheath with its tip positioned
in the distal SVC under fluoroscopic guidance. Position of the catheter was
confirmed by a fluoroscopic spot film of the chest. The peel-away sheath and
guidewire were then removed. The catheter was secured to the skin, flushed,
and a sterile dressing applied.
The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

1.  The accessed vein was patent and compressible.
2.  Basilicvein approach single lumen right PICC with tip in the distal SVC.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of a right 43 cm basilic approach single lumen PowerPICC
with tip in the distal SVC.  The line is ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in with right upper belly pain and fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. The pain started a few days ago, and yesterday I had chills and a high fever. It’s been constant, not coming and going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had this kind of pain before with your liver condition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it feels similar to when I had cholangitis last month. I finished antibiotics then, but I never really felt back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Given your history, we’re concerned it might be another flare. We’ve started you on IV meropenem to cover for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good. But my last infection wasn’t confirmed, right? The scans were normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re being cautious because of your PSC and cirrhosis. Even if the signs aren’t classic, we don’t want to miss an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. My energy has been so low, and I’ve just felt off since last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fatigue could be from ongoing inflammation. We’ll monitor your labs closely. Your white count was low last night, which is common in cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver numbers? The alkaline phosphatase was high last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your Alk Phos is elevated again—264—along with mild AST/ALT rise. That supports possible cholangitis, even without duct dilation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we’re treating it as cholangitis even if the scan doesn’t show it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your symptoms, fever, and lab trends point that way. We’ll get an MRCP tomorrow to look more closely at your bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds right. I just want to make sure we’re not missing something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’re also holding your diuretics for now to protect your kidneys while we treat the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’ve reviewed your MRCP from this morning. It shows no bile duct dilation or signs of acute cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not cholangitis? But I had a fever and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The imaging doesn’t show it, but your clinical picture—fever, pain, elevated liver enzymes—still suggests infection. We’re continuing antibiotics for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood cultures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All three came back negative. No bacteria grew. But in patients like you, cultures aren’t always positive, so we don’t rule out infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. So we’re treating based on symptoms, not the test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And your fever has come down since starting antibiotics, which supports that we’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I felt worse before the IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your liver enzymes are starting to improve. Alk Phos is down to 261.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. And the pain is much better—only mild now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re thinking of transitioning you to a different antibiotic that’s easier to give at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Meropenem has been working. Is the new one just as strong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, ertapenem is similar and only needs one dose a day. Much easier than the current twice-daily meropenem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll still need IV, right? Not oral?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, IV. So we’ll place a PICC line tomorrow to finish your 14-day course at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many PICCs. The last few didn’t last long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. The radiology team is experienced and will use ultrasound to find the best vein. We’ll do everything to make it work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, the PICC line was placed successfully this morning in your right arm. It’s in the superior vena cava and ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll switch you to ertapenem today and watch for a dose. If all goes well, you’ll be discharged with home health support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll keep taking my other meds—rifaximin, ursodiol, the diuretics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all of them. We’re restarting your furosemide and spironolactone. And we’re increasing lactulose to three times a day as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had confusion, but I’ll take it as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And keep using hydroxyzine for itching. The skin excoriations suggest you’re still having some pruritus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been worse on my chest lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re looking well. Your exam is much improved—no abdominal tenderness, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. No fever, and the pain is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are stable. White count is low but unchanged, and liver enzymes are trending down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll finish ertapenem for 14 days total. A nurse will come to give the IV dose daily and check the PICC site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a hepatology visit in two weeks. Also, don’t forget your yearly colonoscopy—we’ll send a referral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to schedule it. And if I get fever or pain again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your liver team or go to the ER. Also watch for swelling, shortness of breath, or confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure everything is set up for a smooth transition home. Get some rest and take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with primary sclerosing cholangitis and cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B) was admitted for right upper quadrant pain and fever, concerning for recurrent cholangitis. Despite negative blood cultures and an MRCP showing no biliary dilation or acute cholangitis, she was treated with IV meropenem due to clinical signs of infection. Her symptoms improved, liver enzymes trended downward, and she became afebrile. A PICC line was placed for outpatient IV antibiotic therapy, and she was transitioned to ertapenem to complete a 14-day course. Diuretics were restarted, and lactulose was increased for hepatic encephalopathy prophylaxis. She was discharged home with home health support, instructions to continue all chronic medications, and follow-up with hepatology and for colonoscopy screening.
